newsitem.title: USA: Reich cites moral obligation for minimum wage hike.
newsitem.headline: Reich cites moral obligation for minimum wage hike.

text.p: On the day that 4.2 million minimum wage workers got a raise, Labour Secretary Robert Reich declared Tuesday that the country has a moral obligation to keep people who work hard clothed, fed and sheltered.

Slipping into his academic persona, Reich set aside the economic arguments he has used repeatedly in his three-year quest for a minimum wage hike and lectured students about the philosophical reasoning behind his push for an increase.

"It is a moral obligation," Reich told a George Washington University audience. "We should not have people who are working hard, playing by the rules and not earning enough simply to live on in this society."
The federal minimum wage for an estimated 4.2 million American workers rose by 50 cents Tuesday to $4.75 an hour, the first phase of a 90-cent raise enacted by Congress.
The remaining 40 cents of the increase will take effect next Sept. 1, lifting the pay of nearly 10 million workers to $5.15 an hour, the Labour Department said.

Reich, a former Harvard University professor, stepped away from his lectern and used every inch of his floor space to dramatise his point that "an implicit moral code operates just under the surface of our otherwise impersonal economy."

While Americans are willing to allow market forces to decide most of what happens in this economy, he said there are exceptions -- sweatshops, pension abuses, unsafe working conditions and discrimination -- where society insists on imposing minimum standards.
The minimum wage is one of the those exceptions, he said.

"This implicit moral code stands for the simple proposition that anyone who works hard should earn at least enough to keep themselves and their immediate families clothed, fed and sheltered," Reich said.
"Hence, we now have a minimum wage which, when coupled with a refundable earned-income tax credit, will accomplish this bare requisite of decency," he added.

Before Tuesday's increase, the old $4.25 minimum wage was near a 40-year low in inflation-adjusted terms. Reich has often cited the need to raise it as a key component in his comprehensive plan to close the widening gap between high- and low-income workers.
He stressed, however, that closing the rich-poor gap remains a challenge for the future that will take years and require greater investment in education and training.

Reich advocated a minimum wage hike within the Clinton administration as soon as he took office in 1993. But the effort was set aside while the administration focused on its failed health care reform plan.

The administration-backed 90-cent minimum wage hike that was proposed in early 1995 appeared doomed in the face of staunch Republican opposition until this spring, when an advertising campaign by organised labour, election year politics and overwhelming public support revived it.
Congressional minimum wage backers also commemorated the day the raise took effect.
Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle and other key senators who fought for the increase, led by Sen. Edward Kennedy, D-Mass., hailed the rise.
They were flanked by tables displaying baby food and groceries needed by a young family that could be purchased by the additional $20 a week a family would receive.
The senators emphasised that the increase, amounting to $1,800 a year, was enacted despite intense opposition by leaders of the Republican majority.
